content.title: Chuck Norris dies at 86 after sudden hospitalization
content.text: Chuck Norris’ family has announced his sudden passing, sharing a heartfelt message on Instagram that described the beloved actor and martial arts icon as a man of deep faith, devotion, and kindness. The statement said Norris died peacefully yesterday morning, surrounded by loved ones.What to Know:Norris died at 86 yesterday morning after being hospitalized within the last 24 hours on Kauai.The Norris family confirmed his death on his personal Instagram in a post, calling it a “sudden passing.”They said he was “at peace” and with family at the time.Sources previously said he was alert, joking, and recovering well.He had been training as recently as Wednesday, March 18, maintaining the fitness regimen he followed throughout his life.Earlier this month, he celebrated his birthday with a video showing him boxing with a sparring partner.His filmography spans more than five decades, including cult classics such as The Way of the Dragon, Lone Wolf McQuade, Missing in Action, Invasion U.S.A., and The Delta Force.Norris’ return to the big screen in The Expendables 2 introduced him to a new generation of fans.Admirers across the world are mourning his death and celebrating his legacy as one of Hollywood’s most enduring action figures.Related ReadingHow Chuck Norris Became the Internet’s First Meme and Myth - NewsweekChuck Norris’ Family Statement in Full After Action Legend’s Death - NewsweekThis live blog is now closed, but read on for Chuck Norris' life and legacy.In a polarized era, the center is dismissed as bland. Join today.Mar 20, 2026 at 03:34 PM EDTStrongman Eddie Hall pays tribute to Chuck NorrisTributes to Chuck Norris continued to grow on Friday, with retired British strongman Eddie Hall calling the late action star “an absolute legend of a man.” Hall, who shared his message on Instagram, said the two had “just started to message each other” and that he had hoped to meet Norris in person.Hall reflected on Norris’ enduring image as a symbol of strength, a reputation amplified over the years through viral memes portraying him as unbeatable. Norris’ family echoed that sentiment earlier this week, describing him as “a symbol of strength” in their public statement.“He just turned 86 and looked fantastic,” Hall wrote, adding that the news of Norris’ death “makes you cherish your loved ones a bit harder when stuff like this happens.”Mar 20, 2026 at 03:21 PM EDTStephen King says one Chuck Norris film ‘scared hell’ out of himAuthor Stephen King, known for some of the most iconic horror novels of the last half‑century, says one Chuck Norris movie managed to rattle even him. In a social‑media post, King praised Norris’ performance in the 1982 thriller Silent Rage, writing that the film “scared hell out of my boys…and me.”The movie features Norris as a small‑town sheriff confronting a nearly unstoppable killer with the ability to self‑heal — a premise that blends action with slasher‑style horror. King said he thought Norris was “great” in the role.The writer also shared a few of his favorite Chuck Norris jokes, including: “Chuck doesn’t flush the toilet, he scares the s*** out of it.” In another post, he added: “When he was born, Chuck Norris drove his mother home from the hospital.”Mar 20, 2026 at 03:08 PM EDTHow ‘Chuck Norris facts’ became one of the Internet’s first viral joke formatsThe wave of Chuck Norris jokes that swept the internet in the early 2000s — known as “Chuck Norris Facts” — became one of the first truly global meme formats, transforming the action star’s tough‑guy persona into a form of digital folklore. The jokes took the shape of short, hyperbolic one‑liners that exaggerated Norris’ strength, invincibility and stoic masculinity to absurd extremes.The earliest “facts” circulated on message boards and humor sites, with classics like:“When the Boogeyman goes to sleep, he checks his closet for Chuck Norris.”“Chuck Norris doesn’t wear a watch. He decides what time it is.”“When Chuck Norris does pushups, he pushes the earth down.”As the format evolved, fans pushed the exaggeration even further, inventing feats that defied physics and logic — from Norris breaking the speed of light with a roundhouse kick to burning fire by rubbing ice cubes together. Others played on his supposed toughness in relationships and mythology, including the long‑running joke that Superman wears Chuck Norris pajamas.The phenomenon grew so large that Norris himself eventually joined in. According to a widely cited interview, his personal favorite was: “They tried to put Chuck Norris’s face on Mount Rushmore, but the granite wasn’t tough enough for his beard.”The jokes became a cultural shorthand, appearing on Facebook, Reddit, late‑night shows and even in political campaigns. Their endurance speaks to the simplicity and flexibility of the format — and to Norris’ unique place in pop culture as a symbol of exaggerated, good‑humored toughness.Mar 20, 2026 at 02:55 PM EDTRep. Don Bacon honors Chuck Norris’ Air Force service after actor’s deathRepresentative Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican and Air Force veteran, paid tribute to Chuck Norris following news of the actor’s death, highlighting his military service before his rise to fame. In a post on social media, Bacon noted that Norris served as an Air Policeman during the Cold War and reached the rank of Airman First Class.“I’m saddened to hear of his passing and thank him for his service and legacy,” Bacon wrote, emphasizing the martial‑arts star’s roots in the U.S. Air Force — the period in which Norris first discovered the discipline that would shape his career.Mar 20, 2026 at 02:42 PM EDTWATCH: Chuck Norris’ legacy ahead of deathMar 20, 2026 at 02:29 PM EDTChuck Norris’ philanthropy reached far beyond the dojoChuck Norris’ legacy extended far beyond film and martial arts. Beginning in 1990, he built a significant philanthropic footprint through organizations designed to support children, veterans, and vulnerable communities around the world.Norris founded the United Fighting Arts Federation and Kickstart Kids, a program created to help at‑risk middle and high school students build confidence, discipline, and focus through martial‑arts training. The initiative was designed as a proactive alternative to drug pressure and gang involvement, giving young people a structured path toward personal growth. Kickstart Kids has since become one of the most enduring youth‑development programs tied to a major public figure.Norris and his wife also operated a ranch in Navasota, Texas, where they bottled water under the CForce brand. A portion of the proceeds supported environmental causes and helped fund Kickstart Kids, further linking his business ventures to his charitable mission.His philanthropy extended well beyond youth programs. Norris supported organizations such as Funds for Kids, the Veterans Administration National Salute to Hospitalized Veterans, the United Way, and the Make‑A‑Wish Foundation, contributing through donations, appearances, and fundraising efforts. His advocacy for hospitalized veterans was deeply personal, shaped by his own service in the U.S. Air Force. In recognition of his work, he received the Veteran of the Year award at the American Veteran Awards in 2001.Norris’ charitable reach was international as well. In India, he supported the Vijay Amritraj Foundation, helping fund pediatric HIV/AIDS homes in Delhi, a school for the blind in Karnataka, and care centers for HIV‑positive adults and mentally ill patients in Cochin.Mar 20, 2026 at 02:16 PM EDTWhat was Chuck Norris’ political stance?JERUSALEM, ISRAEL - FEBRUARY 8: (ISRAEL-OUT) In this handout image supplied by the Government Press Office, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ...Chuck Norris was not only a martial‑arts champion and action‑movie icon — he was also one of the most outspoken conservative figures in American entertainment. Over several decades, Norris used his platform to champion right‑leaning causes, endorse candidates, and write opinion columns that reflected his political worldview.Norris’ political identity took shape in the 1980s, when he publicly praised President Ronald Reagan and described himself as a “flag waver” who valued strong leadership. His comments during the release of Missing in Action and The Delta Force reflected his concerns about terrorism and U.S. foreign policy, warning that America’s passive approach would invite future attacks.Beginning in the 2000s, Norris became a regular columnist for the conservative website WorldNetDaily, where he wrote about national security, religion, and cultural issues. His commentary included skepticism about President Barack Obama’s birth certificate, criticism of same‑sex marriage, and warnings about what he described as the spread of “Sharia law” in the United States.Norris frequently endorsed Republican candidates. He backed Mike Huckabee in the 2008 and 2016 primaries, supported John McCain and later Mitt Romney, and voiced approval for Sarah Palin. He also endorsed candidates in state and local races, including Roy Moore in Alabama’s 2017 Senate special election and Larry Elder during California’s 2021 gubernatorial recall effort. In 2007, he visited U.S. troops in Iraq, a trip that underscored his long‑standing support for the military.His political involvement extended beyond U.S. borders. Norris visited Israel and publicly supported Benjamin Netanyahu during the country’s 2013 and 2015 elections.While his positions often sparked debate, Norris remained consistent in his message: a belief in strong national defense, traditional values, and outspoken patriotism. His political voice became as much a part of his public identity as his roundhouse kicks and action‑hero persona.Mar 20, 2026 at 02:03 PM EDTChuck Norris’ military roots and the honors that defined his careerBefore he became a global action star, Chuck Norris built the foundation of his discipline and fighting philosophy in the U.S. military. Serving in the 15th Air Force, 22nd Bombardment Group, and 452nd Troop Carrier Wing, Norris rose to the rank of Airman First Class. It was during this period, while stationed in Korea, that he began studying martial arts — training that would shape the rest of his life.Norris went on to earn an extraordinary collection of black belts across multiple disciplines, including a 10th‑degree black belt in the Chuck Norris System (formerly Chun Kuk Do), a 9th‑degree in Tang Soo Do, an 8th‑degree in Taekwondo, a 5th‑degree in Karate, a 3rd‑degree in Brazilian jiu‑jitsu, and a black belt in Judo. His competitive career was equally decorated: he won the Professional Middleweight Karate Championship in 1968 and held the title for six straight years, earned Karate’s triple crown in 1969, and was named Black Belt magazine’s Fighter of the Year the same year.As his film and television career took off, so did the accolades. Norris received the Action Star of the Year award in 1982, a Hollywood Walk of Fame star in 1989, and the International Box Office Star of the Year honor in 1992. Texas embraced him as one of its own, naming him a Texas legend in 1997, awarding him honorary Texas Ranger status in 2010, and later declaring him an Honorary Texan.His contributions to martial arts were formally recognized with inductions into the Martial Arts History Museum Hall of Fame and the World Karate Union Hall of Fame, along with a Golden Lifetime Achievement Award. The U.S. military also honored him: in 2007, he was named an honorary United States Marine.Even in later years, tributes continued. A 2020 biography celebrated his lifelong commitment to martial arts, and in 2024, a small statue of Norris was installed in Budapest — a testament to his global cultural reach.From Air Force serviceman to world champion to international icon, Norris’ list of honors reflects a career built on discipline, reinvention and enduring influence.Chuck Norris's Star, Hollywood Walk of Fame - August 11th, 2017 - Hollywood Boulevard, Los Angeles, California, CA, USAMar 20, 2026 at 01:50 PM EDTHow Chuck Norris created two global martial-arts styles that still thrive todayBeyond his fame as an action star and cultural icon, Chuck Norris left a lasting imprint on the martial‑arts world by founding two major systems: American Tang Soo Do and the Chuck Norris System, formerly known as Chun Kuk Do. Together, they reflect his evolution from Air Force serviceman to world champion to global instructor.American Tang Soo Do: Norris’ First SystemNorris created American Tang Soo Do in 1966, blending the Moo Duk Kwan style of Tang Soo Do he learned in Korea with elements of judo and Japanese karate traditions such as Shito‑ryu and Shotokan. The hybrid style grew rapidly as Norris opened schools across California, and over time, his black belts and their students continued to refine and expand the system. It became the foundation of his early teaching career and the springboard for his later innovations.The Chuck Norris System: A Modern, Comprehensive StyleIn 1990, Norris formally launched a second system, originally called Chun Kuk Do (“Universal Way”), later renamed the Chuck Norris System. Built on his Tang Soo Do roots, the style evolved as Norris incorporated techniques from a wide range of disciplines he studied during his competitive years — including Goju‑ryu, Kyokushin, Enshin, Brazilian jiu‑jitsu, judo, Arnis, Taekwondo, Hapkido, and American Kenpo.The result is a well‑rounded curriculum emphasizing self‑defense, sparring, grappling, weapons training, and physical conditioning. The system also includes a personal code of honor drawn from Norris’ own values, stressing discipline, loyalty, open‑mindedness, and respect.A Global CommunityThe United Fighting Arts Federation (UFAF), which oversees the Chuck Norris System, has produced more than 3,000 black belts and maintains nearly 4,000 active members worldwide. Each year, practitioners gather in Las Vegas for a major training conference and world championship tournament.Mar 20, 2026 at 01:37 PM EDTHow Bruce Lee and Chuck Norris turned a Colosseum showdown into cinema legendAmerican martial artist Chuck Norris with Chinese American martial artist, actor, director and screenwriter Bruce Lee on the set of his movie Meng Lon...Bruce Lee’s famous instruction to “be formless, shapeless, like water” helped define him as both a martial‑arts innovator and a philosopher, a dual identity that shaped his rise in the late 1960s and early ’70s. As he disrupted Hollywood with roles in Batman, The Green Hornet and later his own films, Lee became a global force — a performer whose physical mastery was matched by a restless, analytical mind.One of the clearest expressions of that blend came in 1972’s Way of the Dragon, the film Lee wrote, directed and starred in. Shot partly in Rome, it showcased his ambition to push martial‑arts cinema into new territory. At the center of the movie was a showdown that would become one of the most enduring fight scenes in film history: Bruce Lee vs. Chuck Norris, then a rising American karate champion making his feature debut.Norris played Colt, a formidable enforcer whose presence gave Lee the kind of equal‑and‑opposite foil he rarely had on screen. Their climactic battle in the Roman Colosseum — balletic, brutal and meticulously choreographed — elevated both men into international icons and sparked a decades‑long debate among fans about who would win in a real fight.Behind the scenes, the rivalry was real but rooted in mutual respect. Norris later recalled that Lee personally phoned him to offer the role, joking that he planned not just to beat the world champion on screen but “kill the world champion.” Lee, for his part, had publicly boasted that he could handle top karate fighters “like a parent would a young child,” a comment that reflected his confidence more than hostility.Norris consistently spoke of Lee with admiration, calling him “formidable,” “lightning fast,” and “incredibly strong for his size.” He emphasized Lee’s open‑minded approach to combat — his belief that no single style was supreme and that every discipline had strengths worth absorbing.Asked years later whether he could have beaten Lee in a real competition, Norris sidestepped the bravado with a line Lee himself might have delivered: “Showing off is the fool’s idea of glory.”Mar 20, 2026 at 01:24 PM EDTNetanyahu mourns Chuck Norris, calling him a ‘great friend of Israel’Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu paid tribute to Chuck Norris following the actor’s death at 86, describing him as both “a great friend of Israel and a close personal friend.” In a message posted on social media, Netanyahu said he and his wife, Sara, were “deeply saddened” by the news.Norris, long admired in Israel for his martial arts achievements and his iconic role in Walker, Texas Ranger, maintained warm ties with the country over the years. Netanyahu highlighted not only Norris’ global fame but also the personal warmth he brought to millions of fans.Mar 20, 2026 at 01:11 PM EDTWho are Chuck Norris’ kids? All about Mike, Eric, Dina, Dakota and DanileeIn a photo from 2012, actor Chuck Norris, wife Gena O'Kelley, and their children arrive at the premiere of Expendables 2 held at Grauman's Chinese The... | Photo by Frank Trapper/Corbis via Getty ImagesChuck Norris, who died Friday at age 86 in Hawaii, was known worldwide as a martial arts champion and action‑movie icon. But away from the screen, he was a father of five — a family that spanned two marriages and an early relationship, each chapter reflecting a different stage of his life and career.Norris and his first wife, Dianne Holechek, welcomed two sons during their 30‑year marriage. Their eldest, Mike Norris, born in 1962, followed closely in his father’s footsteps. He built a career as an actor, director and stunt performer, appearing in films and television projects, including work connected to Walker, Texas Ranger. Their second son, Eric Norris, born in 1965, carved out his own path behind the scenes as a stuntman and stunt coordinator before competing professionally as a NASCAR driver.Norris also fathered a daughter, Dina, in the early 1960s from a relationship outside his marriage. He wrote in his memoir that he learned of her years later, and the two eventually formed a relationship. Dina has largely remained outside the public eye.In 1998, Norris married Gena O’Kelley, a former model and actress. The couple welcomed fraternal twins in 2001: Dakota Alan Norris and Danilee Kelly Norris. The twins were raised mostly out of the spotlight, appearing only occasionally alongside their parents.While some of Norris’ children embraced careers in entertainment and stunt work, others chose private lives. Together, they reflect the wide‑ranging personal legacy of a man whose public persona was defined by toughness, discipline and decades of cultural influence.Read more here.Mar 20, 2026 at 12:58 PM EDTChuck Norris shared heartbreaking final post ahead of his deathJust days before his death, Chuck Norris shared a light‑hearted and heartfelt message with fans on Instagram, marking what would become his final public post. The action star celebrated his 86th birthday with trademark humor, writing, “I don’t age. I level up,” alongside a sunny clip of himself enjoying a bit of playful outdoor action.Norris thanked fans for their decades of support, saying their encouragement meant more to him than they would ever know. He also expressed gratitude for his health, his long career, and the chance to keep doing what he loved. The post ended with a simple, warm sign‑off: “God Bless, Chuck Norris.”The message now reads as a poignant farewell from a performer whose toughness, discipline and generosity made him a beloved figure across generations.Mar 20, 2026 at 12:45 PM EDTDanilee Norris honors her father as ‘my safe person’ in emotional tributeDanilee Norris, the daughter of Chuck Norris and Gena O’Kelly, shared a heartfelt message mourning her father’s death, calling him her “safe person these past 24 years.” In an Instagram post, she reflected on the bond they shared from the moment she was born.“My dad was my protector the moment I was born and as soon as he took me in his arms, I've always been his little girl,” she wrote, describing a relationship defined by deep affection and unwavering support.Danilee said her father “loved so deeply and cared for every single person in his life with so much tenderness,” adding that behind his tough public persona was “a heart… full of love.”“To say I am thankful for him being my dad is an understatement,” she said, closing her tribute with gratitude for the man she described as both a warrior and a gentle presence in her life.Mar 20, 2026 at 12:31 PM EDTChuck Norris’ net worth at the time of his death at 86Chuck Norris, the martial arts champion and Walker, Texas Ranger star who died on March 19, 2026, at age 86, left behind a legacy that stretched from competitive karate to Hollywood stardom — and a substantial fortune built over six decades in the public eye.As of early 2026, Norris’ net worth was widely estimated between $70 million and $100 million, reflecting the breadth of his career. His earnings came from a mix of blockbuster action films, long‑running television success, bestselling books, fitness endorsements, and a steady stream of commercial partnerships that kept him culturally relevant well into his later years.Norris’ financial success was rooted in the same discipline that defined his martial arts career. Before becoming an actor, he was a six‑time undefeated World Professional Middleweight Karate champion and founded the United Fighting Arts Federation, which has awarded thousands of black belts worldwide. His business ventures — from martial arts schools to branded products — added to his long‑term wealth.In his final years, Norris lived with his family on a ranch outside Houston, a property that became central to his lifestyle and public image. It was there that he continued to write, train, and occasionally appear in films, most recently in the 2024 sci‑fi action movie Agent Recon.Mar 20, 2026 at 12:18 PM EDTInside Chuck Norris’ 1990s breakthrough: box office dominance and the rise of ‘Walker, Texas Ranger’By 1990, Chuck Norris had become one of Hollywood’s most reliable action stars, with his films collectively earning more than $500 million worldwide. His blend of martial arts intensity and stoic, lone‑wolf charisma drew comparisons to both Bruce Lee and Clint Eastwood, earning him nicknames like the “blonde Bruce Lee” and aligning his screen persona with Eastwood’s iconic Dirty Harry.As MGM absorbed the Cannon Films library, Norris continued collaborating with his brother Aaron Norris, who directed him in a string of early‑1990s projects including Delta Force 2, The Hitman, Sidekicks (1993), Hellbound (1994), Top Dog (1995), and Forest Warrior (1996).His biggest cultural milestone arrived in 1993 with the launch of Walker, Texas Ranger. Norris starred as Sgt. Cordell Walker, a Texas Ranger who battled criminals with a mix of martial arts, frontier justice, and moral clarity. The CBS series became a ratings powerhouse, running for eight seasons and consistently ranking among the network’s top programs through the late 1990s. The show spawned the 1999 spinoff Sons of Thunder and a crossover with Sammo Hung’s Martial Law.Outside of Walker, Norris appeared on the Randy Travis special Wind in the Wire (1993), served as a special enforcer at WWF’s Survivor Series in 1994, and published The Secret Power Within in 1996. Beginning in 1997, he also became a familiar face in long‑running Total Gym infomercials alongside Christie Brinkley.In 1998, CBS premiered Logan’s War: Bound by Honor, a television film starring Norris that ranked among the week’s most‑watched broadcasts. By the end of the decade, Norris had firmly established himself as both a television fixture and one of America’s most enduring action icons.Mar 20, 2026 at 12:04 PM EDTWhat to know about Chuck Norris’ ex-wife Dianne Holechek, his high-school sweetheart and partner through his rise to fameChuck Norris And Dianne Holechek Attend The Variety Clubs Salute To Burnett on November 23, 1982 (Photo by Ralph Dominguez/MediaPunch via Getty Images...Dianne Holechek, the first wife of Chuck Norris and the mother of two of his children, died in December 2025 at age 84 after a long battle with dementia. Her death was announced by Norris and their eldest son, Mike, who said she passed peacefully at her home in Texas.Holechek and Norris were high‑school sweethearts in Torrance, California, beginning their relationship in the mid‑1950s. They married young — she was 17, he was 18 — just as Norris entered the U.S. Air Force. Their early years together were marked by long separations and personal challenges, including Norris later acknowledging he fathered a daughter outside the marriage in 1962. Despite the strain, the couple built a family and welcomed two sons, Mike in 1962 and Eric in 1965.As Norris’ martial arts career took off and eventually led him to Hollywood, Holechek pursued her own ventures, including running a successful restaurant. The couple remained together for three decades, with Norris often crediting their stability to her willingness to travel with him during filming. They separated in 1988 and finalized their divorce the following year.Even after their split, Norris said they remained “close friends,” continuing to co‑parent and stay involved in each other’s lives. Announcing her death, he wrote that her kindness, intelligence and devotion to their sons “will never be forgotten.”Mike Norris told TMZ his mother was “the best, the greatest mom,” adding that the family was grateful her suffering had ended. Holechek leaves behind a legacy intertwined with Norris’ early life and career, remembered by her family as a loving mother and a steady presence during the years when Norris became a global action star.Mar 20, 2026 at 11:51 AM EDTChuck Norris’ later-career projects, books, endorsements and pop-culture legacy: What to knowBeginning in 2006, Chuck Norris shifted into a new phase of his career, expanding his work as an author, cultural figure and commercial personality while continuing to make selective screen appearances. He published the Western novel The Justice Riders in 2006, followed by a sequel co‑written with the same team. Around the same time, the explosion of “Chuck Norris Facts” online led to a wave of books, including Ian Spector’s The Truth About Chuck Norris, which became a bestseller. Norris briefly sued the publisher before dropping the case, later releasing his own officially endorsed collection, The Official Chuck Norris Fact Book.Norris continued writing, releasing the political book Black Belt Patriotism in 2008, which reached the New York Times bestseller list. That year also saw the release of Chuck Norris: Bring On the Pain, a mobile game inspired by his internet fame. In 2010, he began a nationally syndicated column for Creators Syndicate, focusing on health and public policy.Throughout the 2010s, Norris became a familiar face in global advertising campaigns, appearing in commercials for T‑Mobile, World of Warcraft, Toyota, Hoegaarden, United Healthcare, and numerous international brands. He returned to the big screen in 2012 with The Expendables 2, a global hit, and launched CForce Bottling Co. with his wife after discovering an aquifer on their Texas ranch.Norris’ pop‑culture presence continued into the late 2010s and 2020s. He served as a brand ambassador for Fiat’s commercial vehicles, inspired another mobile game (Nonstop Chuck Norris), hosted the History Channel documentary Chuck Norris’ Epic Guide to Military Vehicles, and made a cameo in the series finale of Hawaii Five‑0. In 2021, he appeared as a playable character in World of Tanks during a holiday event.Across books, commercials, games and television, Norris’ later‑career output reinforced his status as both an enduring action icon and a uniquely self‑aware figure in American pop culture.Mar 20, 2026 at 11:38 AM EDTHere are the Chuck Norris projects you may or may not know aboutIn the early 2000s, Chuck Norris expanded his screen presence beyond action films, returning to television as a covert operative in the CBS movies The President’s Man (2000) and its sequel A Line in the Sand (2002). He also appeared in the faith‑based drama Bells of Innocence (2003) and made a comedic guest appearance on the sitcom Yes, Dear that same year.Norris reached a new generation of fans in 2004 with a memorable cameo in DodgeBall: A True Underdog Story, playing himself as a tournament judge. The film became a major box‑office hit, and that year he also released his autobiography Against All Odds: My Story.In 2005, Norris launched the World Combat League, a team‑based full‑contact martial arts competition that supported his Kickstart Kids charity. He briefly returned to his signature TV role in Walker, Texas Ranger: Trial by Fire, a CBS movie continuation of the long‑running series.Around the same time, the internet phenomenon known as “Chuck Norris Facts” exploded in popularity. Created by college student Ian Spector, the satirical one‑liners exaggerated Norris’ toughness and invincibility. Rather than distancing himself, Norris embraced the joke, sharing his favorites publicly and even incorporating the meme into talk‑show appearances and morale‑boosting visits with U.S. troops in Iraq.Mar 20, 2026 at 11:25 AM EDTTexas Gov. Greg Abbott calls Chuck Norris a ‘legend’ in tribute after actor’s deathTexas Gov. Greg Abbott paid tribute to Chuck Norris following the actor’s death at 86, calling him a “legend” whose influence stretched far beyond Hollywood. In a statement posted on social media, Abbott said “all of Texas mourns” the loss of the Walker, Texas Ranger star, praising both his cultural impact and his connection to conservative audiences.Abbott highlighted Norris’ long career as a martial arts champion and action icon, noting that his portrayal of Cordell Walker helped define Texas toughness for a generation. He also credited Norris with energizing conservative voters, saying the actor “electrified generations… giving them a passion and voice to fight for the principles that make America the greatest nation on earth.”The governor described Norris as embodying “toughness, grit, and patriotism,” qualities he said reflected the spirit of Texas itself.Mar 20, 2026 at 11:06 AM EDTHow Chuck Norris became one of the Internet’s first global mythsChuck Norris promoting the move "Pumping Iron" in Sicily, Italy, on July 24, 1985. | Frederic Meylan/Sygma via Getty ImagesChuck Norris’ death at 86 is prompting tributes across generations — a reflection not only of his long career in martial arts and television, but of his second life as one of the internet’s earliest and most enduring memes. Long before social media turned celebrities into viral shorthand, Norris became something new: a digital folk hero.His real‑world biography already read like a myth. Norris discovered martial arts while serving as an Air Force air policeman in South Korea, then rose to become a dominant champion. That authenticity — the sense that his toughness was earned, not manufactured — became the foundation for the exaggerated persona that would later flourish online.Hollywood amplified that image. His breakout turn as Colt, Bruce Lee’s adversary in The Way of the Dragon, and his long run as the morally unshakeable Cordell Walker in Walker, Texas Ranger cemented him as a symbol of uncomplicated strength. On television, justice was swift, violence was clean, and the hero never wavered.In the mid‑2000s, the early internet seized on that certainty and inflated it into absurdity. “Chuck Norris facts” — short, hyperbolic jokes about his invincibility — spread across forums, emails, and early social platforms:Chuck Norris does not sleep. He waits.Chuck Norris has two speeds: Walk and kill.The flu gets a Chuck Norris shot every year.The format was simple, endlessly adaptable, and instantly global. It turned Norris into one of the first universally recognized meme archetypes, a symbolic unit of power that transcended language and culture.Read more here.Mar 20, 2026 at 10:58 AM EDTChuck Norris’ Cannon Films era and 1980s action peak'Missing in Action' or 'Portés disparus' 1984 directed by Joseph Zito. (Photo by Sunset Boulevard/Getty Images)Chuck Norris entered the height of his 1980s stardom with Missing in Action (1984), the first film in his long‑running collaboration with Cannon Films. Playing Col. James Braddock, Norris headlined a Vietnam POW‑rescue thriller that became a major box‑office hit and cemented him as the studio’s marquee action star. He later dedicated the trilogy to his younger brother Wieland, who was killed in Vietnam in 1970.That same year, Norris began work on Code of Silence, a Chicago‑set police thriller directed by Andrew Davis. The film marked a dramatic shift for Norris, earning some of the strongest reviews of his career. Critics praised its grounded tone and Norris’ restrained performance, with The New York Times calling it a potential breakout moment. The film opened at No. 1 and ultimately grossed more than $20 million.Norris continued his momentum with Missing in Action 2: The Beginning (1985), a prequel exploring Braddock’s captivity, followed by the explosive Invasion U.S.A. later that year.In 1986, he co‑starred with Lee Marvin in The Delta Force, another Cannon hit centered on an elite counterterrorism unit. That year also saw the debut of Karate Kommandos, a short‑lived animated series featuring Norris as a cartoon action hero, along with a Marvel comic adaptation.Norris closed out 1986 with Firewalker, an action‑adventure comedy co‑starring Louis Gossett Jr. The film showcased a lighter side of Norris, who said he wanted to stretch beyond his stoic persona. Reviews were mixed, but the film earned more than $11 million.By the late 1980s, Norris was expanding beyond film. He published the bestselling memoir The Secret of Inner Strength (1987), then returned to his Braddock character in Missing in Action III (1988), directed by his brother Aaron. That same year, he starred in Hero and the Terror, playing a detective hunting a serial killer.Mar 20, 2026 at 10:45 AM EDTChuck Norris’ 1979–1983 action breakthrough cemented his rise as a leading manChuck Norris’ ascent as a bankable American action star accelerated between 1979 and 1983, a period that produced several of his most influential early films. He began with A Force of One (1979), playing a world karate champion who aids police in a murder investigation. Despite having no studio backing, the independently released film earned more than $20 million, surpassing the success of Good Guys Wear Black and proving Norris’ growing draw at the box office.He followed with The Octagon (1980), a thriller centered on a terrorist network trained in ninja combat. This time, studios took notice, and American Cinema Releasing distributed the film, which brought in nearly $19 million. Norris continued his momentum with An Eye for an Eye (1981), directed by Steve Carver.In 1982, Norris headlined Silent Rage, an action‑horror hybrid and his first film released by a major studio, Columbia Pictures. That same year, MGM signed him to a three‑picture deal and released Forced Vengeance, though creative differences led to the contract’s cancellation.His true breakout of the era came with Lone Wolf McQuade (1983), produced by Orion Pictures and again directed by Carver.
